section_summary: This section traces U.S. reporting on Japanese narcotics control from May 1930 through November 1931. It covers the League of Nations inquiry into opium smoking in Taiwan and the Kwantung Leased Territory, alleged bulk narcotics advertisements and international smuggling, Japan’s 1930 narcotics ordinance, and seizure statistics for 1928. The latter half contains State Department questionnaires and Japanese government answers describing the opium monopoly, licensing, import-export certification, inspection, recordkeeping, and enforcement; the final questionnaire continues beyond page 80.

subfiles.title: Traffic in Narcotics—Japan jacket cover
subfiles.about: File-jacket cover identifying the case as traffic in narcotics in Japan.
subfiles.summary: File jacket Traffic in Narcotics—Japan, dated May 6, 1930, with case-control information.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on the League opium inquiry
subfiles.about: Cross-reference to a report from Japan concerning the Commission of Inquiry into Opium Conditions.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a May 1930 report on the League opium commission's visit to Japan and its findings.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 184 on the Commission of Inquiry into Opium Conditions
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, for the U.S. ambassador at Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports on the League of Nations commission’s visit and evaluates Japan’s opium monopolies in Taiwan and the Kwantung Leased Territory.
subfiles.summary: Neville reports the League commission found, in Taiwan and Dairen, many unregistered smokers and smuggling, with Kwantung conditions worse; Japanese monopoly control had not reduced opium smoking.

subfiles.title: Letter identifying the Spot Goods Reporter
subfiles.from: Anslinger, Secretary, Federal Narcotics Control Board
subfiles.to: John K. Caldwell, Department of State
subfiles.about: Identifies the Japanese trade paper and approximate issue date in which bulk cocaine advertisements reportedly appeared.
subfiles.summary: Anslinger tells Caldwell the cocaine advertisements reportedly appeared in the Spot Goods Reporter in February 1930; American officers in Japan might locate the issue.

subfiles.title: Instruction No. 70 concerning narcotics advertisements in Japan
subfiles.from: Francis White, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: Edwin L. Neville, American chargé d’affaires ad interim, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Requests an informal investigation of reported Spot Goods Reporter advertisements offering enormous quantities of cocaine and morphine.
subfiles.summary: Instruction No. 70 quotes press reports of advertisements for 100 and 1,000 tons of cocaine in Tokyo and asks the embassy to investigate the publication, firms, drug source and buyers.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 215 on the status of the Spot Goods Reporter
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, American chargé d’affaires ad interim, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Replies that the original Spot Goods Reporter had ceased publication but that a clandestine narcotics advertising sheet may still circulate.
subfiles.summary: Neville says the Spot Goods Reporter apparently ceased in 1922 or 1923; he finds no sanctioned illicit manufacture, though Kobe and other ports served as transshipment points.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Despatch No. 215 to the Treasury Department
subfiles.about: Transmits the Tokyo embassy’s findings concerning the Spot Goods Reporter.
subfiles.summary: State sends Treasury Despatch No. 215 of July 26, 1930 on the alleged Yokohama publication advertising narcotics.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 235 transmitting Japan’s narcotics-control ordinance
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, American chargé d’affaires ad interim, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Forwards a translation of Japan’s May 1930 Regulations for the Control of Narcotic Drugs and comments on their strengths and weaknesses.
subfiles.summary: Neville calls Ordinance No. 17, implementing the 1925 Geneva Convention, a significant advance, but criticizes the five-gram sales exemption and lagging administration.

subfiles.title: Regulations for the Control of Narcotic Drugs, Department of Home Affairs Ordinance No. 17
subfiles.about: Translation of Japan’s comprehensive ordinance regulating narcotics manufacture, coca cultivation, trade, transportation, and enforcement.
subfiles.summary: The ordinance defines controlled drugs, including morphine, heroin, cocaine, ecgonine derivatives, Indian hemp, and designated preparations. It establishes permissions and reporting for manufacture and coca cultivation, as well as import and export authorizations and controls over transit, landing, reshipment, and transshipment. Dealers must label most packages, verify purchasers, preserve certificates and transaction books, and submit to inspection. The final articles establish cancellation powers, imprisonment and fines, vicarious liability, and transitional provisions repealing earlier controls.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Despatch No. 235 and Ordinance No. 17
subfiles.about: Forwards the embassy despatch and translation of Japan’s Regulations for the Control of Narcotic Drugs.
subfiles.summary: State sends Treasury Despatch No. 235 and a translation of Ordinance No. 17 (May 19).

subfiles.title: Country of origin of drugs found in illicit traffic in Japan during 1928
subfiles.from: Japanese Government, communicated by the League of Nations Advisory Committee on Traffic in Opium and Other Dangerous Drugs
subfiles.about: Lists 1928 Japanese customs seizures by drug, quantity, origin, sender, port, and seizure date.
subfiles.summary: Bilingual table of 1928 seizures at Yokohama, Kobe, Osaka, Moji and Nagasaki of morphine, heroin and opium linked to Rotterdam, Dairen, Paris and Shanghai.

subfiles.title: Drugs seized by Japanese customs authorities during 1928
subfiles.about: Reports the quantities and origins of narcotic drugs seized in Japan, Korea, and the Kwantung Leased Territory in 1928.
subfiles.summary: Memorandum on drugs seized by Japanese customs in 1928 in Japan, Korea and Kwantung, with origins including Germany and Switzerland, mostly benzoylmorphine.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 122 enclosing a clipping on an international narcotics ring
subfiles.from: W. Cameron Forbes, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Forwards an Osaka Mainichi clipping about a Yokohama investigation into narcotics smuggling.
subfiles.summary: Forbes encloses a clipping about a Yokohama District Court investigation of an international narcotics ring.

subfiles.title: “Coded Cables Seized Reveal Big Dope Ring”
subfiles.about: Reports allegations of a London-centered international narcotics ring using air and sea routes through Yokohama.
subfiles.summary: Clipping: Procurator Ito seized over 100 coded cables from an Osaka druggist; traffickers allegedly moved drugs from Europe through Yokohama to Dairen, Shanghai and Hong Kong in a traffic worth over 80 million yen.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Despatch No. 122 to the Commissioner of Narcotics
subfiles.to: Secretary of the Treasury, for the Commissioner of Narcotics
subfiles.about: Forwards the Tokyo despatch and Osaka Mainichi clipping about an alleged international drug ring.
subfiles.summary: State sends Despatch No. 122 and its clipping to Treasury for the Commissioner of Narcotics.

subfiles.title: Diplomatic Serial No. 1097: Laws and Regulations Regarding the Control of the Traffic in Narcotic Drugs
subfiles.from: W. R. Castle Jr., for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: American diplomatic officers and certain American consular officers
subfiles.about: Directs overseas posts to verify and supplement questionnaires on narcotics-control laws throughout metropolitan and dependent territories.
subfiles.summary: Circular asks posts to correct questionnaires on narcotics laws, including colonies and mandates, for U.S. enforcement and a planned international reference; lists territories assigned to consular posts.

subfiles.title: Japan questionnaire on legal and administrative measures for narcotics control
subfiles.to: American Embassy at Tokyo and Japanese authorities
subfiles.about: Questionnaire summarizing known Japanese narcotics laws and seeking corrections and detailed administrative information.
subfiles.summary: The form reviews Japan’s opium monopoly, controlled substances, administrative agencies, licensing, professional eligibility, and import-export certification. Draft answers describe the Home Affairs Department, prefectural governors, police and customs cooperation, postal shipments, bonded warehouses, dealer records, prescriptions, reporting, annual inspections, illicit-traffic reporting, and penalties. Many questions remain unanswered or are marked for clarification, showing that the document was intended for official Japanese review. The questionnaire also identifies Yokohama, Kobe, Osaka, and Moji as principal narcotics ports.

subfiles.title: Instruction No. 127 requesting coverage of the South Sea Islands Mandate
subfiles.to: American chargé d’affaires ad interim, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Requests a separate report on narcotics law in the South Sea Islands Mandate.
subfiles.summary: Instruction No. 127 directs the Tokyo embassy to report separately on narcotics law in the South Sea Islands Mandate as well as Japan proper.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 398 transmitting revised Japanese questionnaire answers
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, for the U.S. ambassador at Tokyo
subfiles.about: Forwards the Japanese government’s rewritten answers concerning narcotics control in Japan and the mandated islands.
subfiles.summary: Neville reports that Japanese authorities preferred to rewrite the entire questionnaire rather than make numerous small corrections to the American draft. He encloses their series of answers and states that Japan’s narcotics laws also applied to the Mandated Islands.

subfiles.title: Revised questionnaire answers on narcotics control in Japan proper
subfiles.about: Begins Japan’s official rewritten answers on its narcotics laws, monopoly, administration, authorized businesses, and licenses.
subfiles.summary: The response supplies a corrected list of laws and explains the government monopoly over raw and medicinal opium, including poppy licensing, laboratories, designated buyers, and distribution through prefectural governors. It describes the Department of Home Affairs, Opium Commission, inspectors, police and customs coordination, and the rules governing pharmacists, manufacturers, druggists, importers, and exporters. It names authorized opium- and coca-alkaloid manufacturers and gives their Tokyo and Osaka addresses. The final pages set out licensing applications, investigation and revocation procedures, purchaser certification, postal shipment rules, and the absence of special narcotics taxation; the response continues beyond page 80.
